title: Why Would God Put a Fence Around Something He Created So Beautiful?
paragraphs: Why Would God Put a Fence Around Something He Created So Beautiful?

Sex was never God’s dirty secret. It was His gift. And understanding why Scripture places it inside marriage may completely change the way you see desire, purity, your body, your past—and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is something strange about the way Christians sometimes talk about sex.
We whisper about it.
We blush around it.
We warn teenagers about it.
We preach against its misuse.
And somewhere along the way, people can walk away with the impression that God created human sexuality and then immediately became embarrassed by His own invention.
But that cannot be the biblical story.

Before pornography existed, before adultery shattered homes, before lust became an industry, before dating apps, secret messages, casual hookups, broken vows, hidden browser histories, and lonely people learned to use another human body as temporary medicine for an aching soul...
there was Eden.
And before there was sexual sin, there was sexual goodness.
God created the human body.
God created attraction.
God created marriage.
God created the possibility of a husband and wife knowing one another with an intimacy so profound that Scripture reaches for language stronger than merely saying they became physically close.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ ... וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-davaq be-ishto ... ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
He clings to his wife...
and they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”

That word davaq carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, adhering. Even the translation tradition preserves that force: Genesis 2:24 is rendered “hold fast,” “be joined,” or “be united” across major English translations.
Notice the order.
Leave.
Hold fast.
Become one flesh.
Sex does not create the whole marriage covenant, but biblically it belongs inside that covenantal union. It is bodily language expressing something much larger than bodily pleasure.
And suddenly the Christian sexual ethic begins to make more sense.
God did not reserve sex for marriage because sex is filthy.
He reserved sexual union for marriage because it is profoundly significant.
We often protect worthless things carelessly and valuable things carefully.
You don't put a diamond in the driveway and complain that the jewelry box is restricting it.
You protect what is precious precisely because it is precious.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop.
Because maybe nobody ever taught you this.
Maybe you were only told:
“Don't.”
Don't have sex.
Don't lust.
Don't cross the line.
Don't sleep together before marriage.
But nobody explained the beauty behind the boundary.
So eventually the boundary looked arbitrary.
Maybe even cruel.
“If we love each other, why would God care?”
“We're committed.”
“We're practically married.”
“Nobody is getting hurt.”
“Times have changed.”
And underneath those questions is often another one:
Why would a loving God care what consenting adults do with their bodies?
Jesus gives us an important answer.
When questioned about marriage, Christ did something remarkable.
He went backward.
Back beyond contemporary culture.
Back beyond human preference.
Back to creation.
Jesus quoted Genesis and said that a man leaves father and mother, is joined to his wife, and “the two shall become one flesh.” Then He added:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus did not treat marriage as an arbitrary social invention.
He rooted it in God's creative intention.
And the New Testament keeps doing the same thing.
Hebrews says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure.
Paul tells believers to flee sexual immorality because their bodies belong to God, have become temples of the Holy Spirit, and were “bought at a price.” His conclusion is intensely physical:
“Therefore honor God with your bodies.”
That changes everything.
Christianity does not say your body is meaningless.
It says almost the opposite.
Your body matters so much that Jesus purchased you at the cost of His blood.
Your sexuality matters.
What you do with another person's body matters.
What you allow another person to do with yours matters.
Your private life matters.
Your desires matter.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God loves people.
The biblical vision refuses to reduce another human being to an experience.
Sex says something with the body.
It says closeness.
Nakedness.
Knowledge.
Trust.
Giving.
Receiving.
Vulnerability.
Union.
“One flesh.”
That is why Scripture refuses to pretend sex is merely recreation involving two bodies.
Paul makes this almost startlingly clear in 1 Corinthians 6.
Speaking about prostitution—not marriage—he warns that sexual intercourse creates a real “one flesh” involvement, quoting Genesis itself: “The two will become one flesh.”
Think about what that means.
Paul's argument only works because sex is not meaningless.
The modern world often tells us that sex can simply be physical.
Scripture says the body cannot be separated so neatly from the person.
You are not a soul temporarily renting some disposable biological machinery.
Your body is part of you.
So God cares about sexual holiness because God cares about you.
And He cares about the person you desire.
This is also why biblical sexuality can never be reduced to “wait until the wedding and then anything goes.”
Marriage does not turn selfishness into holiness.
A marriage certificate is not permission to exploit another person's body.
Biblical marital intimacy must exist within the wider commands of Christlike love, faithfulness, mutual care, honor, and self-giving.

Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. Then, astonishingly, he quotes Genesis 2:24 again and connects the mystery of marriage with Christ and His church.
So Christian marriage is not merely two people finally receiving religious permission to have sex.
It is covenant.
Faithfulness.
Sacrifice.
Belonging.
Service.
A lifelong union in which sexuality finds its intended covenantal home.
Sex is not the foundation of marriage.
Christlike covenant love is.
And sexual intimacy becomes one beautiful expression within it.
But now we have to enter the room most Christian articles quietly avoid.
The room where somebody is reading this with tears beginning to form.
Because theology is easy until it collides with memory.
Maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe many times.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe you didn't.
Maybe somebody introduced you to sexuality before you were old enough to understand what was happening—and what happened to you was not your sin.
Maybe pornography became your secret anesthesia.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel chosen.
Maybe you gave your body because you were terrified they would leave.
Maybe you were told, “If you really love me...”
Maybe you convinced yourself you were basically married.
Then the relationship ended.
And they walked away carrying memories of a version of you that you wish you could retrieve.
Maybe you are married now, but pornography followed you into the marriage.
Maybe there is an affair nobody knows about.
Maybe there are messages on your phone that would devastate your spouse.
Maybe you keep promising God:
“This is the last time.”
And then comes another night.
Another search.
Another compromise.
Another morning staring at the ceiling wondering how somebody who loves Jesus can keep returning to something that leaves them feeling so divided inside.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not begin by pretending sin isn't sin.
But neither does it end by leaving sinners where they fell.
One of the most beautiful sentences in Paul's discussion of serious sin comes immediately after a devastating list.
After naming sexual immorality alongside other sins, Paul turns toward redeemed believers and says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes the Gospel thunder:
“You were washed... you were sanctified... you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Read that again.
Not because your past doesn't matter.
Because Jesus can change what your past gets to mean.
Christian purity is not the boast of people who never became dirty.
Christian purity ultimately rests upon Christ cleansing sinners.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
The first says:
“My sexual choices don't matter.”
The cross answers:
Sin matters enough that Christ died.
The second says:
“My sexual past has ruined me beyond redemption.”
The cross answers:
Grace is powerful enough that Christ rose.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by calling darkness light.
He rewrites everything by entering our darkness, bearing sin at Calvary, conquering death, forgiving repentant sinners, and beginning the work of making them new.
Maybe you cannot become someone who never committed that sin.
But in Christ you can become someone no longer ruled by it.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem tomorrow.
You cannot make yourself innocent by pretending nothing happened.
But Christ can justify the guilty.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by collecting enough good behavior to outweigh your failures.
But the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
And this is why God's design for sex is ultimately not about deprivation.
It is about worship.
Paul's conclusion is not merely:
“Stop having immoral sex.”
It is:
Glorify God in your body.
Your body can become an altar of obedience.
That means the unmarried Christian who says no when desire screams yes can worship God with that no.
The boyfriend who refuses to pressure his girlfriend can worship God with restraint.
The girlfriend who refuses to trade her convictions for someone's affection can worship God with courage.
The engaged couple who establish boundaries because they want Christ more than immediate gratification can worship God while waiting.
The husband who shuts down the secret account can worship God through repentance.
The wife or husband who confesses hidden sexual sin rather than continuing a double life can begin walking toward truth.
The person who closes pornography and reaches for accountability can worship God in the battle.
The Christian who has fallen and comes crawling back to Jesus can worship through repentance.
And married couples can worship God by cultivating an intimate life marked by faithfulness, tenderness, mutual honor, patience, generosity, and love.
God's command is not:
“Desire nothing.”
It is:
Let Me teach your desires where home is.
And that is harder.
Because sometimes obedience hurts.
Singleness can hurt.
Waiting can hurt.
Being thirty, forty, fifty, or older and still unmarried can hurt.
Watching friends build families while your prayers seem unanswered can hurt.
Wanting touch does not make someone spiritually defective.
Wanting companionship is not automatically idolatry.
Loneliness is real.
Sexual desire can be powerful.
Scripture does not need us to pretend otherwise.
But Christianity makes an audacious claim:
Jesus Christ is worthy of obedience even when obedience costs us something.
We do not obey God because every command immediately feels comfortable.
We obey because He is Lord.
And because the One giving the command is also the One who gave Himself for us.
The hands asking you to surrender are scarred hands.
That matters.
Purity without Jesus becomes pride for those succeeding and despair for those failing.
But holiness centered on Jesus produces something different.
Humility.
Repentance.
Dependence.
Grace.
You stop asking merely:
“How close can I get to sin without technically sinning?”
And begin asking:
“How completely can this part of my life belong to Christ?”
That question changes dating.
It changes marriage.
It changes what you watch.
It changes what you send.
It changes what you fantasize about.
It changes what happens when nobody is watching.
It changes how you see another person's body.
It changes how you see your own.
And maybe tonight the greatest battle is not whether you understand the theology.
Maybe you understand it perfectly.
Maybe the real battle is whether you believe Jesus is better than the thing you keep running toward.
That is where surrender begins.
Not:
“Jesus, make me less human.”
But:
“Jesus, make every part of my humanity Yours.”
Your eyes.
Your hands.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your hormones.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your relationships.
Your sexuality.
Your future marriage, if He gives you one.
Your singleness, for however long He asks you to carry it.
All of it.
His.
And if you've fallen, don't confuse repentance with self-hatred.
Repentance means turning.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Break secret patterns.
Seek wise pastoral accountability where needed.
End relationships that continually pull you away from Christ.
Put practical boundaries around devices, conversations, places, and circumstances where you repeatedly fall.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into permission to surrender completely.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is great.
There may be consequences from yesterday that grace does not instantly erase.
There may be trust that takes time to rebuild.
There may be wounds requiring patient healing.
Forgiveness does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
But your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps this article found you because somebody shared it.
Think about that.
Someone else's small act of pressing “share” may have carried biblical truth into the exact moment you needed it.
So don't let this stop with you.
Someone's teenager may need this.
Someone's unmarried friend may need it.
Someone's marriage may need it.
Someone trapped in pornography may need it.
Someone convinced their sexual past has disqualified them from Jesus may desperately need to hear that the Gospel still says:
“Such were some of you... but you were washed.”
Not because typing words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the battle into the light is the first crack in the wall secrecy built around you.
Scripture calls believers to generosity and Gospel partnership; it does not give any ministry permission to turn support for itself into a test of devotion to Christ.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because people need Jesus.
The person who reads what you shared tomorrow may never tell you what they almost did tonight.
And perhaps that's the thought worth carrying with you:
Your body is not too dirty for Christ to redeem, your desire is not too strong for Christ to rule, and your story is not too scandalous for grace to write another ending.
